headline: Google drops on Gemini 4 safety restrictions while the ASX closes up 0.79% — NRL Grand Final Sunday is Roosters vs Knights at Accor Stadium.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slid 1.87% last night with no major company-specific catalyst — broader market caution and profit-taking across growth/gaming stocks likely weighed in. The long-term thesis remains intact: GTA VI is still the most anticipated game release in years. No structural reason to panic.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google fell 1.71% last night despite launching its impressive new Gemini 4 Argon model. The market reacted negatively to news that Google is restricting access to the model over safety concerns — investors worry about the revenue delay when a blockbuster product is held back. The underlying AI story remains strong.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara bounced 1.37% today, a welcome green day after a tough stretch. No single catalyst stands out — likely a combination of broader ASX strength (the index was up 0.79%) and some relief buying after heavy prior losses. The lithium market remains under pressure, so this is a small positive in an ongoing tough environment.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI edged up 0.17% today on the ASX, riding the general market uplift. The Google Gemini 4 Argon launch is a positive signal for AI sector sentiment, though the safety access restrictions tempered enthusiasm slightly.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG nudged up 0.21% today, consistent with the broader ASX gain. As a diversified multi-asset ETF, it just quietly does its job — small daily moves like this are totally normal.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS edged up 0.08% today on the ASX, reflecting a modest positive carry-through from last night's slightly positive US session. The S&P 500 finished up 0.19% last night, so this is broadly in line.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE dipped 0.16% today — a tiny move. Emerging markets continue to be buffeted by China's fuel export halt and Middle East tensions, but this is well within normal daily noise for an EM fund.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft was essentially flat last night, down just 0.02%. Microsoft just posted a trillion-dollar quarter driven by AI cloud revenue, and the stock continues to hold its ground near all-time highs. Barely a blip.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Gemini 4 Argon is huge — but the safety restrictions are the catch
watch_today.detail: Google launched Gemini 4 Argon, reclaiming the benchmark lead over OpenAI and Anthropic in coding and reasoning — but then immediately restricted access over safety concerns. The stock dropped 1.71% last night as a result. For a long-term holder, this is frustrating but not alarming — Google's AI position is clearly strong, and the restriction is about responsible rollout, not a product failure. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: TTWO: Down 1.87% last night — still no fundamental reason to sell
watch_today.detail: Take-Two slipped 1.87% last night on no specific bad news. The stock is still 12.3% below your entry price overall, but the long-term investment case (GTA VI launch, massive game pipeline) hasn't changed. A rough night isn't a reason to exit. This is a hold for patient investors.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: A welcome bounce, but lithium pain isn't over yet
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals bounced 1.37% today, a positive sign — but the stock is still down 45% on your total investment. The lithium market remains oversupplied globally and there's no near-term catalyst to change that. Hold if you believe in the long-term lithium demand story (EVs, batteries), but manage expectations for continued volatility.

watch_today.title: RBA hiked rates — and now CBA's boss thinks they're done
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates again (a first in 15 years at this level), but Commonwealth Bank CEO Matt Comyn told the market he thinks the hike cycle is now finished. That's significant — if the RBA is done, borrowing costs stabilise, which is good for growth assets and property. Watch how this plays out for your broader portfolio this week.

watch_today.title: Middle East escalation: third US aircraft carrier deployed
watch_today.detail: The US is sending a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as Trump weighs new military strikes. Crude oil is already elevated at US$91.26/barrel. If conflict escalates further, oil could spike — that flows through to inflation and could complicate the RBA's 'done hiking' story. Worth keeping an eye on.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI sector momentum is building — consider topping up on dips
watch_today.detail: The GXAI ETF was up slightly today and the AI sector is buzzing after Google's Gemini 4 Argon launch. You're currently down 7.66% on this position, but the long-term AI growth story is intact and arguably getting stronger. If you have spare cash and a long time horizon, any further dip could be a reasonable top-up opportunity.

world.summary: The Middle East is the biggest global story right now, with a third US aircraft carrier deployed and oil prices elevated. China's fuel export halt is becoming a geopolitical flashpoint, and US electoral integrity concerns are intensifying ahead of midterms.

stories.title: Third US Aircraft Carrier Heads to Middle East as Trump Weighs New Strikes
stories.why_it_matters: The US is deploying a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East — an extraordinary show of force — as President Trump actively considers launching new military strikes in the region. This follows existing tensions involving Iran-linked groups and ongoing conflicts. Three carrier groups in one theatre is a level of US military commitment not seen in years. Oil has already risen on the news, and an escalation could send energy prices sharply higher, affecting everything from petrol prices to inflation globally.

stories.title: China's Fuel Export Halt: Beijing Using Energy as Geopolitical Leverage?
stories.why_it_matters: China has halted fuel exports, a move analysts say could be Beijing deliberately using energy supply as a geopolitical weapon — similar to how Russia used gas exports to pressure Europe. Countries that rely on Chinese refined fuel products are now scrambling. For Australia, which has close trade ties with China, this is a development worth watching — it adds to global energy market uncertainty at exactly the wrong time, when the Middle East is already unsettled.

stories.title: Trump Doesn't Rule Out Declaring State of Emergency Before Midterm Elections
stories.why_it_matters: President Trump has refused to rule out declaring a national state of emergency in the lead-up to the US midterm elections — a move that would give the White House sweeping executive powers and could dramatically affect how the elections are run. Separately, his administration is accused of quietly making it harder for US citizens living abroad to vote, with Democrats filing a lawsuit over changes to Pentagon voter registration forms. Experts are warning that efforts to investigate election threats have also been quietly abandoned. Together, these moves are raising serious alarm bells about the integrity of the upcoming midterms.

stories.title: Brazil Government Calls for Probe into US Funding of Far-Right Causes
stories.why_it_matters: Brazil's government is demanding an investigation into what it says is US money flowing to far-right political movements inside Brazil. This is a significant diplomatic flashpoint between the two largest economies in the Americas and suggests growing international pushback against what many governments see as American interference in domestic politics. It adds to a pattern of strained US relations with allied nations under the current Trump administration.

stories.title: Jared Kushner's Financial Stake in Israeli Defence Firms Raises Conflict of Interest Concerns
stories.why_it_matters: A new report reveals that Jared Kushner — Trump's son-in-law and close advisor — holds significant financial stakes in Israeli defence companies, at the same time as the Trump administration is actively weighing military action in the Middle East. Critics say this is a textbook conflict of interest: Kushner personally profits from Israeli defence spending while advising a president on Middle East military decisions. The report is drawing significant attention from ethics watchdogs and opposition lawmakers.

markets.summary: The ASX had a solid day, closing up 0.79% to 8,682. Last night on Wall Street, the S&P 500 edged up 0.19% and the NASDAQ was essentially flat. Gold hit a fresh high at US$4,217 an ounce, while crude oil slipped 1.73% to US$91.26 despite Middle East tensions. The Aussie dollar is steady at US$0.6943.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session: a slight gain, with the market holding near record highs despite Middle East uncertainty.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Last night's session: virtually flat. Google's drop on safety concerns offset broader tech stability.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil fell despite Middle East escalation — some profit-taking after recent gains. Still elevated historically.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold continues its run higher, driven by geopolitical uncertainty and safe-haven demand. Another record area.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is barely changed — steady at about 69.4 US cents.

politics.summary: The RBA has hiked interest rates to a level not seen in 15 years, but the CBA boss reckons they're done. Inflation has climbed to 4%, driven by fuel and housing costs. The Albanese government is pushing ahead with AI legislation.

stories.title: RBA Hikes to a 15-Year High — But CBA Boss Says It's the Last One
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised interest rates to a level not seen in 15 years — a significant milestone that shows how seriously the RBA is taking inflation. However, Commonwealth Bank CEO Matt Comyn told the market he believes this is the final hike, and that rates have now peaked. If he's right, that's genuinely good news: mortgage holders get certainty, and financial markets can start pricing in eventual cuts. That said, rates staying high for longer still squeezes household budgets. Watch for the RBA's next statement closely.

stories.title: Inflation Jumps to 4% as Fuel and Housing Costs Climb
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's inflation rate has risen to 4%, above the RBA's 2-3% target band. The main culprits are fuel costs — driven partly by Middle East tensions pushing up global oil prices — and housing costs (rents and mortgage repayments). For everyday Aussies, this means the cost of living squeeze continues. It also complicates the RBA's decision-making: they've just hiked, but inflation is still running hot.

stories.title: RBA Denies Staff Pay Rise to Keep Up with Inflation — Right After Hiking Rates
stories.why_it_matters: In a politically awkward move, the RBA has rejected pay rise requests from its own staff that would have kept pace with inflation — on the very same day it raised interest rates to fight inflation. The optics are poor: the central bank is telling Australians to accept less spending power while refusing to give its own workers real wage growth. It's drawn sharp criticism from unions and Labor MPs, and puts the RBA in an uncomfortable spotlight.

stories.title: Albanese Government Pushes Ahead with AI Legislation
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government says it is 'getting on with the job' of delivering AI legislation for Australia — setting rules for how artificial intelligence can be developed and used, including liability for harms. This comes as AI tools are moving into workplaces, healthcare, and government services at speed. Australia is behind the EU (which has already passed AI laws) but ahead of the US, which still lacks a federal framework. The legislation would affect tech companies, employers using AI tools, and potentially investors in AI-exposed stocks.

ai.summary: Google stole the AI headlines this week with its Gemini 4 Argon model, claiming the top spot over OpenAI and Anthropic on key benchmarks — but it's not yet available to everyone. AI regulation is also heating up globally.

stories.title: Google Launches Gemini 4 Argon — Beats GPT-6 and Claude at Coding, But in Limited Release
stories.why_it_matters: Google officially launched Gemini 4 Argon, its most powerful AI model yet, and it's claiming the top spot on benchmark tests for coding, reasoning, and general intelligence — beating OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. Google is also offering it at aggressive pricing to win over developers and businesses. The catch: it's in limited release only, meaning most users can't access it yet. For investors in GOOG, this is a positive signal that Google is very much in the AI race — but the market reaction was mixed because of the restricted rollout.

stories.title: Google Restricts Access to Gemini 4 Argon Over Safety Concerns
stories.why_it_matters: Despite the impressive benchmark results, Google is limiting who can use Gemini 4 Argon because of unspecified safety concerns — essentially saying the model is powerful enough that they want to be careful about who gets access and how it's used. This is partly responsible for the stock dip last night: Wall Street sees a delay in revenue generation when a flagship product is gated. It's a responsible move, but it costs Google momentum in the race against Microsoft and OpenAI.

stories.title: How Trump's White House AI Accord Works
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump White House has struck a deal with major AI companies — a voluntary 'accord' rather than legislation — covering how AI should be developed and deployed in the US. Unlike the EU's legally binding AI Act, this is a handshake agreement with no enforcement mechanism. Critics say it's toothless; supporters say it avoids stifling innovation with red tape. For Australian investors in US tech stocks, the key takeaway is that the US federal government is unlikely to impose heavy AI regulation any time soon.

stories.title: Senator Hawley Calls for AI Liability Laws — A Rare Bipartisan Push
stories.why_it_matters: Republican Senator Josh Hawley is pushing for new AI regulations that would make tech companies legally liable for harm caused by their AI systems — a significant shift from the industry-friendly stance most Republicans take. If AI liability laws passed, companies like Google and Microsoft could face lawsuits for AI-generated misinformation, deepfakes, or harmful outputs. It's an early-stage proposal, but it's notable because it's coming from the right side of US politics, suggesting there may eventually be bipartisan appetite for some form of AI accountability rules.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is set — Roosters vs Knights on Sunday at Accor Stadium. AFL trade season has kicked off and end-of-season awards are in. The Koori Knockout tournament is underway.

stories.title: NRL Grand Final: Roosters vs Knights — Sunday 6:30pm at Accor Stadium
stories.why_it_matters: It's Grand Final week! The Sydney Roosters will face the Newcastle Knights this Sunday, 4 October, at Accor Stadium with a 6:30pm kick-off. It's shaping up as a blockbuster — the Knights are chasing their first premiership since 2001, while the Roosters are hunting another title for their star-studded roster. A massive occasion for rugby league fans.

stories.title: NRL Stars Leaving En Masse — Myth Debunked About Player Loyalty
stories.why_it_matters: A big post-season exodus of NRL stars is underway, with multiple high-profile players switching clubs or retiring after the season. News.com.au takes a look at the wave of departures and debunks the idea that players stay loyal to one club — with contracts, money, and family driving decisions as much as team loyalty. Expect plenty of transfer news over the coming weeks.

stories.title: 11 Retiring NRL Stars: What's Next? A Boxer, Fashion Mogul and the Next Joe Rogan
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports profiles 11 NRL stars hanging up the boots after this season, with some fascinating post-footy plans — one is pursuing boxing, another is moving into fashion, and at least one wants to become a podcast host in the mould of Joe Rogan. It's a fun look at what elite athletes do after the game, with a bumper crop of retirements headlining this off-season.

stories.title: AFL Trade Season Opens: First Domino Falls, Butters Trade the Big One to Watch
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL trade period has officially opened and the first deal has been completed. The biggest name being talked about is Port Adelaide's Connor Butters, with multiple clubs circling and a potential three-way trade scenario emerging. Fox Sports reports a 'lose-lose' backup option may be needed if talks stall. It shapes as the defining trade of the window — AFL fans will want to watch this one closely over the coming days.

stories.title: Sydney Swans Hand Out End-of-Season Awards
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Swans handed out their 2026 end-of-season awards, capping off the AFL year for the club. The full list of award winners is out — best and fairest, coaches award, and more. Meanwhile, Brisbane Lions named their first club champion for the year, with a 'big-game Lion' capping a golden individual season with the top honour.
